'''''Sisymbrium loeselii''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Brassicaceae]] known by several common names, including '''small tumbleweed mustard''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SILO3|taxon=Sisymbrium loeselii|accessdate=16 November 2015}}</ref> '''false London-rocket''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> and '''tall hedge mustard'''. It is native to Eurasia, and it is known on other continents as an [[introduced species]] and in some areas a common roadside [[weed]].

It is an annual herb producing a hairy, erect stem which can exceed a meter in height. The leaf blades are divided into triangular, lance-shaped, and toothed linear lobes, and are borne on [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]]. The top of the stem is occupied by a [[raceme]] of flowers with bright yellow petals each measuring just under a centimeter long. The fruit is a [[silique]] up to 3.5 centimeters in length containing tiny seeds.

[[File:Flowers of tall hedge mustard (Sisymbrium loeselii) in West Bengal, India.jpg|thumb|Closeup of flowers, in [[West Bengal]], India.]]
This plant is [[allelopathy|allelopathic]] against other species growing around it. It produces chemicals that inhibit the [[germination]] of seeds of other species, including [[Pseudoroegneria spicata|bluebunch wheatgrass]] (''Pseudoroegneria spicata'') and [[Festuca idahoensis|Idaho fescue]] (''Festuca idahoensis'').<ref name=bainard>Bainard, L. D., et al. (2009). Inhibitory effect of tall hedge mustard (''Sisymbrium loeselii'') allelochemicals on rangeland plants and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. ''Weed Science'' 57(4):386-393.</ref> It also inhibits [[arbuscular mycorrhiza]]l fungus species, such as ''[[Glomus intraradices]]''.<ref name=bainard/>

The species is named for German botanist [[Johannes Loesel]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Putnam Park Wildflowers |url=https://www.chem.uwec.edu/putnam/notes-wf-Sisymbrium-loeselii.html |access-date=2025-05-14 |website=www.chem.uwec.edu}}</ref>

== Uses ==
The leaves are spicy enough to make [[wasabi]] but can also be mixed into salads and other dishes.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref>
